title: Routing surface and controlplane divergence notes
body:
Context and intent:
This is a lightweight working note comparing the routing surface and control-plane responsibilities across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. The goal is to enumerate practical differences that affect isolation, tenant routing, and multi-region failure modes so we can surface precise implementation/ops tasks for the runtime and infra teams.

Short summary (one-liner):
- Hosted: centralized control plane, multi-tenant ingress, soft isolation via routing + runtime quotas; easiest to evolve but highest blast radius.
- Dedicated: tenant-reserved capacity (pool-level isolation), control plane still central but with tenant-specific policies; predictable latency/throughput, fewer noisy-neighbor issues.
- Private: local control plane (customer-managed or vpn/VPC), network-level isolation and egress constraints; we defer many routing decisions to customer infra.

Key differences that matter for platform engineering:
1) Control plane locus and responsibilities
   - Hosted: full control-plane features (routing policies, model catalog, rollout gates) are enforced centrally. We perform policy enforcement, region routing, failover logic, and billing attribution.
   - Dedicated: control plane still central for billing, telemetry, and global config, but per-tenant routing hints must be pushed to dedicated pools (policy translation).
   - Private: minimal control plane surface (license/heartbeat + optional telemetry). Customer network + local control layer handle final routing. We must provide a compact policy descriptor (policy-as-data) rather than distributed orchestration.

   Implication: design policy model as a gradient: full-rules -> compiled hints -> compact policy blob. This lets us reuse the same operator UX while simplifying enforcement in Private.

2) Tenant isolation boundaries (what "isolation" means in each mode)
   - Hosted: logical isolation. Tenants share nodes but are isolated by routing, rate limits, namespaces, and cache partitioning where feasible. KV cache must be tenant-keyed to prevent cross-tenant leakage.
   - Dedicated: physical or pool-level isolation. A tenant gets a reserved GPU pool; isolation is at host/pool boundary -- network, disk, and NVMe scratch can be dedicated. Runtime-level multi-tenancy is reduced.
   - Private: isolation is determined by the customer's infra. We must avoid assumptions about egress or shared metadata stores.

   Operations note: For Hosted, ensure per-tenant telemetry identifiers at the earliest ingress hop to enable tracing and safe cache routing. For Dedicated, provide hard boundaries in the allocator (no transparent tenant stuffing).

3) Ingress routing and session affinity
   - Affinity needs differ: low-latency chat workloads want sticky routing to reuse KV cache; embeddings/one-shot workloads tolerate random routing.
   - Hosted: we can implement adaptive affinity in the edge router (cookie/token + short TTL) and fall back to stateless scheduling. Implement TTL-based sticky routing where seq_len and session_id heuristics show >20% token savings.
   - Dedicated: prefer intra-pool affinity (route to same pool) but rely on pool-local scheduler for host selection. Avoid cross-pool affinity to preserve isolation.
   - Private: do not assume any central affinity. Expose guidance and a small client-side library to your private customers for local affinity if they want sticky routing.

4) Multi-region failover and routing policies
   - Hosted: active-active by default with region-aware latency routing. Fallback policy should prefer compatible model variants (smaller/quantized) if region capacity constrained.
   - Dedicated: prefer tenant's home region. If global failover needed, require explicit customer opt-in to spill to other regions.
   - Private: usually single-region; cross-region failover depends on customer network and compliance.

   Pattern recommendation: define a three-tier fallback policy artifact:
     * primary-region policy (strict)
     * cross-region spill policy (opt-in; specify allowed regions and model tiers)
     * degraded-model fallback (compatible variant ids)

5) Routing surface and configuration distribution
   - To minimize divergence, config should be represented in the same canonical format, but we support three delivery modes:
     * Hosted: centrally push policies via control plane; live updates.
     * Dedicated: control plane compiles tenant policies into pool-anchored manifests pushed to pool controllers.
     * Private: export signed policy blobs customers can import; include a human-readable plan and a checksum.

   - Security: signed/blinded policies for Private to avoid leaking global topology.

6) KV/prefix cache coherence and correctness
   - Hosted: cache key includes tenant id, session id, model id. Eviction policies should be tenant-aware.
   - Dedicated: caches can be shared per-tenant pool; lower risk of cross-tenant eviction anomalies.
   - Private: customers may run caches colocated in their infra; document required invariants (tenant id prefixing, atomicity of KV updates) and provide a validation tool.

7) Network egress and security boundaries
   - Hosted: egress controls at edge (per-tenant egress lists, allowed endpoints for tool calls). Need SNI/ALPN-aware firewall rules for policy enforcement.
   - Dedicated: offer per-tenant egress NAT pools or customer-managed egress gateways.
   - Private: we must be explicit that we do not control egress; provide integration guides for common enterprise proxies and HSM/KMS setups.

8) Observability and SLOs
   - Metrics to emit at ingress: tenant_id, route_decision, pool_id, model_variant, sequence_length, latency_ms, token_count.
   - Hosted: central analytics can compute tenant-level SLOs and detect noisy neighbors.
   - Dedicated: split dashboards per-pool with tenant overlays.
   - Private: emit a minimal telemetry bundle; respect opt-out. Provide a local metrics collector that can forward to our ingestion (if permitted).

9) Billing and attribution surface
   - Hosted: attribute at ingress with canonical tenant_id and model_variant. Beware double-counting on retry/fallback.
   - Dedicated: billing counters decoupled from central token-metering; reconcile per-pool usage daily.
   - Private: provide usage-export hooks (S3, syslog) and support reconciliation tools.

10) Runtime fallbacks and graceful degradation
   - Prefer model-variant fallback (same model family, lower precision) before cross-tenant spill.
   - Order of fallbacks (recommended): local pool variant -> other model variant in same pool -> cross-region (if allowed) -> queued with backpressure signal -> 503 with structured reason.

Operational playbook (rough):
- On latency spike in Hosted: check route_decision changes, detect if affinity churn increased, and look for cache-hit regression. If cache hit rate drops by >15% for top 10 tenants, consider increasing affinity TTLs and enabling temporary per-tenant pool pinning.
- On Dedicated pool exhaustion: consult tenant's commit; if overflow allowed, spill to standby dedicated pool assigned to the tenant; if not, inform customer and return structured backpressure.
- On Private telemetry loss: fall back to local control-plane defaults. Ensure policy blobs include safe defaults for routing and no automatic cross-region failover unless explicitly enabled.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Policy schema: draft JSON schema to express affinity hints, allowed spill regions, allowed model variants, egress constraints. (Action: Priya to sketch by 2024-11-01)
- Affinity heuristics: what thresholds make sense for enabling sticky routing? collect production samples. (Action: Liam to run sampling job PLAT-682)
- Private policy signing: how do we rotate keys and revoke policies? (Action: security input needed)
- Compatibility matrix for model variants across regions (we need this for automatic degraded-model fallback).

Notes to self / reminders:
- Keep the public API surface identical, but do not hide the fact that enforcement differs under the hood.
- Document exact guarantees we provide in each mode (consistency, latency, durability) for SRE runbooks and customer-facing docs.

References / links in body:
- Slack: #platform-routing thread - ts: 2024-10-12 (see thread: slack.redwood/team-platform/PLAT-routing-20241012)
- GitHub prototype for affinity router: https://github.com/redwood-inference/route-prototypes/pull/43
- Jira: PLAT-682 (affinity sampling), PLAT-763 (policy schema)

If accepted, next steps:
1) Turn policy sketch into v0 schema and test compile->manifest flow for Dedicated.
2) Implement signed policy export for Private and draft customer import guide.
3) Add per-tenant telemetry at earliest ingress hop (edge) and a dashboard widget for affinity/cache hit KPIs.

-- Aisha
